# Overview {#sec-overview}

This portfolio uses the methods covered in this course on real-world data. I have done 4 projects: project 1 looks at benchmark forecast versus ARIMA models forecast and compares them, project 2 looks at the volatility of bond yields and which GARCH specification describes it best, project 3 uses harmonic regression and project 4 use Hidden Markov Models to find regimes in yield changes and compare the regime modal forecast against a modal that assume errors are I.I.D. and normal. Porject 1,2 and 4 all look at the same data, South African 10-year government bond yields and project 3 looks at the average air temperature in Nottingham. Also, the tutorial questions that I have done have been provided below as well as an AI use log and journal. 

# Data {#sec-data}

I am now going to do some EDA for both datasets. Lets first look at the bond yields dataset.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# packages

library(tidyverse)
library(timetk)
library(tsibble)
library(feasts)
library(fabletools)
library(tibbletime)
library(lubridate)
library(tseries)
library(knitr)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# read the FRED csv and rename columns

za_raw <- read_csv("data/IRLTLT01ZAM156N.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(date = observation_date, yield = IRLTLT01ZAM156N) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), yield = as.numeric(yield)) |>
  arrange(date)

tibble(n = nrow(za_raw),
  start = min(za_raw$date),
  end = max(za_raw$date),
  n_missing = sum(is.na(za_raw$yield))
) |> kable(caption = "Raw series: number of observations, date range and missing values.")

```

The series is the monthly long-term (10-year) government bond yield for South Africa, in per cent per annum. It is compiled by the OECD and distributed by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis as FRED series [IRLTLT01ZAM156N](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IRLTLT01ZAM156N).

A market-determined yield was chosen over an administered policy rate because it is compatible with every method used in the projects.

## Choice of sample period

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# check whether the series is market-determined or administered, by era

za_raw |>
  mutate(
    change = yield - lag(yield),
    # cut on dates rather than years so the first boundary can fall in March 1975
    era = cut(date,
              breaks = as.Date(c("1957-01-01", "1975-03-01", "1986-01-01", "1995-01-01", "2001-01-01", "2009-01-01", "2021-01-01", "2027-01-01")),
              labels = c("pre-March 1975", "1975-85", "1986-94 sanctions era", "1995-2000 pre-targeting", "2001-08 inflation targeting", "2009-20 post-GFC", "2021-26 post-COVID"),
              right = FALSE)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(change)) |>
  group_by(era) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    pct_no_change = round(100 * mean(change == 0), 1),
    n_distinct = n_distinct(yield),
    sd_of_changes = round(sd(change), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Months with zero change by era. A high percentage indicates an administered rate rather than a market-determined yield.")
```

The era boundaries mark changes in South Africa's political and monetary regime: the start of market pricing of government debt, the 1985 debt standstill, the 1994 democratic transition, inflation targeting from 2000, the global financial crisis and COVID-19. They are a working choice, and other boundaries could be defended. Before March 1975 the standard deviation of monthly changes is much lower than in any later era. In that period 86.6% of months show no change and the yield takes only 20 distinct values in 217 months, compared with 10.0% and 110 values in 1975-85 and almost no zero changes afterwards.

From July 1952 the Reserve Bank set a fixed pattern of rates for long-dated government stock and changed it only from time to time. This pattern was abolished from 19 February 1975, after which the Bank dealt in government stock at market-related prices (South African Reserve Bank, 1975). The earlier values are therefore administered quotes rather than market yields, so the sample starts in March 1975, the first full month of market-related pricing.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: false

# restrict to the market-determined period and build both a tibble and a tsibble

start_date <- as.Date("1975-03-01")

za_tbl <- za_raw |>
  filter(date >= start_date)

za_ts <- za_tbl |>
  mutate(month = yearmonth(date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = month) |>
  select(month, yield)

za_tt <- za_tbl |>
  as_tbl_time(index = date)

has_gaps(za_ts) |> as_tibble() |> kable(caption = "Implicit gaps in the monthly index.")
# no gaps, if there are gaps the lag() and difference() functions would skip a missing month, this confirms no missing months.
```

## Summary statistics

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# summary statistics for levels and first differences

bind_rows(
  za_tbl |> summarise(series = "levels", n = n(), mean = mean(yield),
                      sd = sd(yield), min = min(yield), max = max(yield)),
  za_tbl |> mutate(d = yield - lag(yield)) |> filter(!is.na(d)) |>
    summarise(series = "first differences", n = n(), mean = mean(d),
              sd = sd(d), min = min(d), max = max(d))
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "Summary statistics.")
```

From March 1975 to June 2026 (616 months) the yield averages 11.68% with a standard deviation of 3.09 percentage points, and ranges from 6.90% to 18.30%. Monthly changes average -0.001 percentage points, so over the whole sample the yield ends slightly below where it started, and their standard deviation is 0.38 percentage points. The largest fall (1.79) and the largest rise (1.92) are about 4.7 and 5.0 standard deviations from zero, which suggests heavier tails than a normal distribution.

## Time plot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# time plot of the yield with the era boundaries marked

events <- tribble(
  ~ date, ~ label, as.Date("1975-03-01"), "market pricing begins", as.Date("1985-09-01"), "debt standstill", as.Date("1994-04-01"), "democratic transition", as.Date("2000-02-01"), "inflation targeting", as.Date("2008-09-01"), "GFC", as.Date("2020-03-01"), "COVID")

za_tbl |>
  plot_time_series(date, yield, .smooth = FALSE, .interactive = FALSE, .title = "SA 10-year government bond yield", .y_lab = "per cent per annum") +
  geom_vline(data = events, aes(xintercept = date), linetype = "dotted", colour = "lightblue") +
  geom_text(data = events, aes(x = date, y = 19.5, label = label), angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 2.4, colour = "blue")
```

There is no obvious deterministic trend. The yield rises from about 9.5% in 1975 to about 17% by the 1985 debt standstill, stays mostly between 15% and 17% until the late 1990s, and reaches its maximum of 18.3% in 1998. It then falls steeply to about 8% by the mid-2000s, after inflation targeting began, and stays mostly between 7% and 10% until 2020. It rises to about 12% in 2023 and 2024 and falls back to about 9% by 2026. The series moves in long swings lasting years rather than fluctuating around a fixed mean, and each level persists long after it is reached. This is the behaviour expected of a series with a unit root, which the tests below examine formally.

## Monthly changes and volatility

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# first differences and a 24-month rolling standard deviation

roll_sd_24 <- rollify(\(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), window = 24)

za_diff <- za_tt |>
  mutate(change = yield - lag(yield)) |>
  filter(!is.na(change)) |>
  mutate(roll_sd = roll_sd_24(change))

za_diff |>
  plot_time_series(date, change, .smooth = FALSE, .interactive = FALSE, .title = "First differences of the yield", .y_lab = "percentage points")

za_diff |>
  filter(!is.na(roll_sd)) |>
  plot_time_series(date, roll_sd, .smooth = FALSE, .interactive = FALSE, .title = "24-month rolling standard deviation of changes", .y_lab = "percentage points")
```

The first differences fluctuate around zero with no visible trend, but their spread changes over time. The 24-month rolling standard deviation is consistent with non-constant variance, which motivates the volatility models in [Project 2](#sec-project-2). Time-varying conditional variance is compatible with weak stationarity of the changes, provided the unconditional variance is finite, so these plots do not by themselves show that the changes are non-stationary.

The rolling standard deviation is lowest in the late 1970s, at about 0.12 to 0.22 percentage points. It rises to about 0.55 to 0.64 between 1983 and 1987, around the debt standstill, falls to about 0.25 by 1990, and reaches its maximum of about 0.74 between 1998 and 2000. After inflation targeting it is mostly between 0.2 and 0.3 from 2004 to 2019, apart from a rise to about 0.4 around the 2008 financial crisis. It jumps to about 0.52 in 2020 and has been about 0.33 since 2022. Because each value uses the previous 24 months, a single large change, such as the rise in early 2020, raises the rolling value for exactly 24 months before it drops out, which produces the flat-topped shapes in the plot.

## Autocorrelation

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ACF and PACF of the levels

za_ts |>
  gg_tsdisplay(yield, plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36) +
  labs(title = "Levels: series, ACF and PACF")
```

The ACF of the levels is close to 1 at lag 1 and decays very slowly and almost linearly, and is still about 0.77 at lag 36. The PACF has a single spike close to 1 at lag 1, a smaller negative spike of about -0.24 at lag 2, and little else. This is the pattern of an autoregressive process with a root at or very near 1, so the levels appear non-stationary and should be differenced. The negative partial autocorrelation at lag 2 is consistent with the positive lag 1 autocorrelation in the changes, discussed next.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ACF and PACF of the first differences

za_ts |>
  gg_tsdisplay(difference(yield), plot_type = "partial", lag_max = 36) +
  labs(title = "First differences: series, ACF and PACF")
```

The changes have one clear autocorrelation, about 0.28 at lag 1. The other autocorrelations are small, and the few at or just beyond the bounds (lag 9 at about -0.10, and lags 21 and 34) are about what is expected by chance among 36 lags tested at the 5% level. The PACF is 0.28 at lag 1 and about -0.12 at lag 2, and then decays quickly with alternating signs. An ACF that cuts off after lag 1 with a decaying PACF suggests an MA(1) for the changes, that is ARIMA(0,1,1) for the levels. An AR(1) would instead show a PACF that cuts off after lag 1. There are no spikes at lags 12, 24 or 36, so there is no sign of seasonality.

## Stationarity tests

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ADF and KPSS tests on the levels and the first differences

lv <- za_tbl$yield
dlv <- diff(lv)

tibble(
  series = c("levels", "first differences"),
  adf_stat = c(adf.test(lv)$statistic, adf.test(dlv)$statistic),
  adf_p = c(adf.test(lv)$p.value, adf.test(dlv)$p.value),
  kpss_stat = c(kpss.test(lv)$statistic, kpss.test(dlv)$statistic),
  kpss_p = c(kpss.test(lv)$p.value, kpss.test(dlv)$p.value)
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "ADF tests the null of a unit root; KPSS tests the null of stationarity. tseries truncates p-values at the ends of its tables.")
```

The ADF test has the null hypothesis of a unit root, and the version in tseries includes a constant and a linear trend. The KPSS test has the null hypothesis of level stationarity. For the levels, the ADF statistic of -2.30 (p = 0.45) does not reject a unit root, and the KPSS statistic of 3.80 rejects stationarity (p < 0.01). For the first differences, the ADF statistic of -9.90 rejects a unit root (p < 0.01), and the KPSS statistic of 0.13 does not reject stationarity (p > 0.10). The two tests agree that the yield is consistent with being integrated of order one. The printed p-values of 0.01 and 0.10 are the limits of the tables that tseries interpolates from, so they are bounds rather than exact values.

## Implications for the projects

The yield is treated as integrated of order one: Project 1 forecasts the levels with one difference, and Projects 2 and 4 model the monthly changes. The ACF of the changes points to an MA(1), which Projects 1 and 2 use for the mean. The changing spread of the changes suggests volatility clustering, which Project 2 tests for and models with GARCH, and the shifts in level and volatility between eras motivate the regime model in Project 4. There is no evidence of seasonality in the changes, which is why Project 1 includes the seasonal naive method only as a check and why the harmonic regression in Project 3 uses a different series.

## Temperature series for Project 3 {#sec-temp-data}

The series is the average monthly air temperature at Nottingham Castle from 1920 to 1939, in degrees Fahrenheit, supplied with R as the `nottem` dataset.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# monthly temperature series (degrees Fahrenheit) and a train/test split, holding out the last 24 months

temp_ts <- datasets::nottem
h_test <- 24
n_train <- length(temp_ts) - h_test
y_train <- window(temp_ts, end = time(temp_ts)[n_train])
y_test <- window(temp_ts, start = time(temp_ts)[n_train + 1])

tibble(set = c("train", "test"),
  n = c(length(y_train), length(y_test)),
  start = c(paste(start(y_train), collapse = "-"), paste(start(y_test), collapse = "-")),
  end = c(paste(end(y_train), collapse = "-"), paste(end(y_test), collapse = "-"))
) |> kable(caption = "Training and test sets.")
```

The last 24 months are held out so that the harmonic regression and the SARIMA in Project 3 can be compared on the same out-of-sample period. The time and seasonal plots show the full series. The numerical checks below use the training set only, so that the held-out months play no part in choosing the model.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# time plot and seasonal plot of the full series
# forecast is not attached until Project 3, because it masks accuracy() from fabletools, which Project 1 relies on

forecast::autoplot(temp_ts) +
  labs(title = "Average monthly air temperature at Nottingham Castle", x = "year", y = "degrees Fahrenheit")

forecast::ggseasonplot(temp_ts) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal plot: one line per year", x = NULL, y = "degrees Fahrenheit")
```

Temperatures follow a strong and regular annual cycle, from about 39°F to 40°F in winter to about 60°F to 62°F in July and August on average. The seasonal plot shows that the shape of the cycle is similar every year: lowest in January or February, rising steadily to a peak in July or August, and falling through the autumn. Individual years differ mainly by a few degrees. The most unusual month is February 1929, the coldest in the series at 31.3°F, and the warmest summers, such as 1921 and 1934, reach about 66°F. There is no visible trend in the time plot.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# monthly summary statistics on the training set

tibble(month = factor(month.abb[cycle(y_train)], levels = month.abb), temp = as.numeric(y_train)) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(temp), sd = sd(temp), min = min(temp), max = max(temp)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |>
  kable(caption = "Monthly temperature summaries, training set 1920 to 1937 (degrees Fahrenheit).")
```

The coldest month on average is February (39.0°F) and the warmest is July (62.1°F), a seasonal range of about 23°F. The standard deviation across years ranges from 1.7°F in April to 3.0°F in December, and tends to be larger in winter and July than in spring and autumn, so the largest variance is about three times the smallest. With only 18 years per month these standard deviations are imprecise, so this is weak evidence against a constant variance, but it is worth checking in the residuals of the Project 3 models.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# annual means remove the seasonal cycle, so a trend would show up directly
# the training set starts in January 1920 and has 18 complete years

annual <- tibble(year = rep(1920:1937, each = 12), temp = as.numeric(y_train)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(mean_temp = mean(temp))

ggplot(annual, aes(year, mean_temp)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", colour = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Annual mean temperature with a fitted linear trend", x = "year", y = "degrees Fahrenheit")

# least squares slope; with 18 annual means the p-value is a rough guide only
trend_fit <- lm(mean_temp ~ year, data = annual)

summary(trend_fit)$coefficients["year", , drop = FALSE] |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(slope = Estimate, se = `Std. Error`, t = `t value`, p_value = `Pr(>|t|)`) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "Linear trend in the annual means (degrees Fahrenheit per year).")
```

The annual means vary between about 47.3°F (1922) and 50.7°F (1921). The fitted slope is 0.047°F per year with a standard error of 0.041 (t = 1.14, p = 0.27), so there is no evidence of a linear trend over 1920 to 1937. With 18 annual means the test has little power, so this shows only that any trend is small relative to the variation between years, not that there is none. The annual means also do not wander in the way a unit root would produce, which supports a constant mean with stationary ARMA errors (d = 0) in Project 3.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ACF of the training series, and of the anomalies left after subtracting each calendar month's mean

anom <- y_train - ave(y_train, cycle(y_train))

forecast::ggAcf(y_train, lag.max = 36) +
  labs(title = "ACF of the training series")

forecast::ggAcf(anom, lag.max = 36) +
  labs(title = "ACF of the monthly anomalies")
```

The ACF of the series is dominated by the annual cycle: it is about 0.8 to 0.87 at lags 12, 24 and 36 and about -0.85 at lags 6, 18 and 30, and it barely decays. This is the pattern a deterministic seasonal component produces, and it hides any other dependence. Once each month's mean is removed, the anomalies have autocorrelations of about 0.27 at lag 1 and 0.16 at lag 2, both outside the bounds, so a warm month tends to be followed by another warm month. Four later lags (12, 24, 28 and 34, all about 0.15 to 0.17 in absolute value) cross the bounds, slightly more than the roughly two expected by chance, but with mixed signs and no consistent pattern. The short-run dependence suggests a low-order autoregressive model for the errors, such as AR(1) or AR(2).

# Projects {#sec-projects}

## Project 1: Forecast comparison for the bond yield {#sec-project-1}

### Summary

- Section and topic: Section 1, benchmark forecasts, ARIMA models and time series cross-validation
- Type: implementation on real-world data
- Question: does a fitted ARIMA model forecast the yield more accurately than simple benchmarks, and at which horizons?
- Data: monthly SA 10-year bond yield from March 1975 (see [Data](#sec-data))
- Methods: naive, drift and seasonal naive benchmarks, non-seasonal ARIMA, expanding-window rolling-origin evaluation at horizons of 1 to 12 months, residual diagnostics
- Key findings: ARIMA(0,1,1) beats the naive forecast only one month ahead, with an RMSE 2.7% lower (0.372 against 0.382 percentage points). From three months on the naive forecast is as accurate or slightly more accurate, drift is worse at every horizon, and the seasonal naive method is far worse at short horizons. The yield behaves close to a random walk, with a small positive correlation between consecutive monthly changes.
- What I would do differently: test whether the accuracy differences are statistically significant, for example with a Diebold-Mariano test, and compare the expanding window with a sliding window to see whether the older data help or hurt.

### Analysis

The comparison is between the naive (random walk) forecast, the drift method, a non-seasonal ARIMA model and, as a deliberate check for seasonality, the seasonal naive method. All are evaluated by rolling-origin cross-validation on the yield in levels.

An expanding window refits each model on all data up to the forecast origin. This is how a forecaster with the full history would work, and it uses as much data as possible for each estimate. A sliding window would adapt faster to regime changes but would discard data that still carry information about the MA coefficient. The 240-month (20-year) initial window, March 1975 to February 1995, gives a stable first estimate and still leaves 365 forecast origins. The naive forecast is the natural benchmark for a series with a unit root, the drift method tests whether a linear trend in the level helps, and the seasonal naive method checks for seasonality. The mean forecast is omitted because the exploratory analysis indicates a unit root, so the historical mean is not a level the yield returns to.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# fable supplies the model functions for the tsibble workflow already in use

library(fable)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# cross-validation settings: initial training window, step between origins, longest horizon

init <- 240
step <- 1
h_max <- 12
```

The ARIMA order is selected once, on the initial training window only, so that the later evaluation data play no part in choosing it.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# automatic non-seasonal ARIMA selection on the initial window

za_ts |>
  slice(1:init) |>
  model(auto = fable::ARIMA(yield ~ PDQ(0, 0, 0))) |>
  fabletools::report()
```

The cross-validation uses ARIMA(0,1,1) without a constant. The order is fixed across origins, while the coefficients are re-estimated at every origin. This matches the order selected on the initial window, and the automatic selection also chose no constant. In a model for the differenced series a constant is a drift, which extrapolates the average monthly change in a straight line. Over the full sample the average change is -0.001 percentage points per month, effectively zero, while over the initial window the yield rose from about 9.5% to about 16%, so a drift fitted there would project rises that did not continue. The higher RMSE of the drift method at long horizons, shown below, is consistent with this.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# expanding window training sets and the four models fitted at each origin

# the last h_max months are dropped so every origin has all horizons observed
za_cv <- za_ts |>
  slice(1:(n() - h_max)) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = init, .step = step)

cv_fits <- za_cv |>
  model(
    naive = NAIVE(yield),
    drift = RW(yield ~ drift()),
    snaive = SNAIVE(yield ~ lag(12)),
    arima = fable::ARIMA(yield ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0))
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# forecasts from every origin, labelled by horizon, and accuracy by horizon

cv_fc <- cv_fits |>
  forecast(h = h_max) |>
  group_by(.id, .model) |>
  mutate(h = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  as_fable(response = "yield", distribution = yield)

cv_acc <- cv_fc |>
  accuracy(za_ts, by = c("h", ".model"))

tibble(origins = n_distinct(za_cv$.id)) |>
  kable(caption = "Number of forecast origins.")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# cross-validated RMSE at selected horizons

cv_acc |>
  filter(h %in% c(1, 3, 6, 12)) |>
  select(h, .model, RMSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = RMSE) |>
  mutate(across(-h, \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Cross-validated RMSE by horizon (percentage points).")
```

At one month ahead ARIMA(0,1,1) is the most accurate method, with an RMSE of 0.372 percentage points, 2.7% lower than the naive forecast (0.382) and 3.1% lower than drift (0.383). At three months ARIMA and naive are equal (0.737). At six and twelve months the naive forecast is best, by about 1% over ARIMA (1.013 against 1.024, and 1.184 against 1.194), with drift worse again (1.033 and 1.233). The seasonal naive method is far worse at short horizons, with an RMSE of 1.230 at one month, more than three times the naive RMSE. At twelve months it equals the naive RMSE exactly, because the seasonal naive forecast twelve months ahead is the last observation, which is also the naive forecast. RMSE grows with the horizon for every method, as expected for a series with a unit root.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# RMSE against horizon for each method

cv_acc |>
  ggplot(aes(h, RMSE, linetype = .model, colour = .model)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:h_max) +
  labs(title = "Cross-validated RMSE by horizon", x = "Months ahead", y = "RMSE (percentage points)", linetype = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# RMSE of each method relative to naive: below one means it beats the random walk

cv_acc |>
  select(h, .model, RMSE) |>
  group_by(h) |>
  mutate(rel_rmse = RMSE / RMSE[.model == "naive"]) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(.model != "naive") |>
  ggplot(aes(h, rel_rmse, linetype = .model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:h_max) +
  labs(title = "RMSE relative to the naive forecast", x = "Months ahead", y = "Relative RMSE", linetype = NULL)
```

Only ARIMA beats the naive forecast, and only at one month, where its relative RMSE is about 0.97. From two months on it is within about 1% of the naive forecast. This follows from the MA(1) structure: the ARIMA forecast differs from the naive forecast only by a fraction of the last one-step error, and beyond one month it stays flat at that adjusted level, so its advantage is confined to the first month. Drift is worse than naive at every horizon, and its relative RMSE rises to about 1.04 at twelve months as the extrapolated trend accumulates. Beyond one month the yield is close to unpredictable from its own past. The differences are also small enough that a formal test would be needed before claiming that any method is more accurate.

The ARIMA model is then fitted to the full sample for diagnostics and a forecast.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# full sample fit and coefficient table

fit_full <- za_ts |>
  model(arima = fable::ARIMA(yield ~ 0 + pdq(0, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 0, 0)))

tidy(fit_full) |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 4))) |>
  # very small p-values print as 0, so show them as < 0.001
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(caption = "Full sample ARIMA estimates.")
```

The full-sample estimate is θ = 0.343 with a standard error of 0.040, giving an approximate 95% interval of 0.27 to 0.42, so the coefficient is clearly positive. It implies a lag 1 autocorrelation of θ/(1 + θ²) ≈ 0.31 in the monthly changes, close to the sample value of 0.28, and since |θ| < 1 the model is invertible. A positive θ means that a surprise this month is partly continued next month: a surprise rise of 1 percentage point raises the forecast of next month's yield by a further 0.34 percentage points above this month's value. One possible source of this correlation is averaging. The OECD describes its long-term rates as generally averages of daily rates (OECD, n.d.), and Working (1960) showed that changes in averages of a random walk have a lag 1 autocorrelation of about 0.25, close to what is observed here. The estimate is lower than on the initial window (0.42), which may reflect sampling variation or a weaker effect after 1995.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# residual diagnostics: plots and a Ljung-Box test

fit_full |>
  gg_tsresiduals(lag_max = 36)

# dof is the number of estimated ARMA coefficients
augment(fit_full) |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 12, dof = 1) |>
  kable(caption = "Ljung-Box test on the ARIMA residuals.")
```

The residual ACF shows no structure: only lag 9 (about -0.10) crosses the bounds, which is expected by chance among 36 lags. The Ljung-Box test on 12 lags, with 11 degrees of freedom after allowing for the MA coefficient, gives Q = 12.30 and p = 0.34, so there is no evidence of remaining autocorrelation. The residuals are centred on zero and roughly symmetric but have heavier tails than a normal distribution, with outliers of about -2.1 in 1998 and +1.9 in 2020. The time plot shows clusters of large residuals in the mid-1980s, around 1998 and in 2020. The residuals therefore look uncorrelated but not independent and identically normally distributed, which affects the prediction intervals rather than the point forecasts.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# 12 month forecast with prediction intervals, shown against recent history

fit_full |>
  forecast(h = h_max) |>
  autoplot(filter_index(za_ts, "2015 Jan" ~ .)) +
  labs(title = "ARIMA forecast of the yield", x = NULL, y = "per cent per annum")
```

These prediction intervals assume a constant innovation variance, which the exploratory analysis suggests does not hold. [Project 2](#sec-project-2) models the variance directly.

### Discussion

At a monthly frequency the yield is close to a random walk. ARIMA(0,1,1) captures a small positive correlation between consecutive monthly changes and improves on the naive forecast by about 3% one month ahead, but not beyond, and neither a drift nor a seasonal pattern helps.

Three limitations apply. First, forecasts from neighbouring origins are based on almost the same data and overlap in the months they forecast, so their errors are correlated and the 365 origins carry less information than their number suggests; the RMSE differences have not been tested formally. Second, the order (0,1,1) was fixed across origins, so the comparison does not reflect uncertainty in model selection. Third, the prediction intervals assume a constant innovation variance, which the residuals contradict, so the intervals are likely too wide in calm periods and too narrow after large shocks.

Natural extensions are a Diebold-Mariano test of the accuracy differences, re-selecting the order at each origin, and combining the mean model with the GARCH variance model of [Project 2](#sec-project-2) so that the prediction intervals widen and narrow with volatility.

## Project 2: Volatility of bond yield changes {#sec-project-2}

### Summary

- Section and topic: Section 1, conditional variance models (ARCH and GARCH)
- Type: implementation on real-world data
- Question: is the variance of monthly yield changes time-varying, and which GARCH specification describes it best?
- Data: monthly changes in the SA 10-year bond yield from April 1975
- Methods: ARMA mean model chosen by information criteria, Ljung-Box and Engle LM tests for ARCH effects, GARCH(1,1) and GJR-GARCH(1,1) with normal and Student t innovations fitted jointly with the mean, robust standard errors, standardised residual diagnostics, news impact curves, volatility forecasts
- Key findings: monthly yield changes show clear ARCH effects (Engle LM test, p < 0.001). GARCH(1,1) with Student t innovations, with about 5.3 degrees of freedom, is preferred by the likelihood, AIC and BIC, and removes the ARCH effects. Volatility is moderately persistent, with a half-life of about 7.5 months, and there is no evidence that rises and falls in the yield affect volatility differently.
- What I would do differently: refit the chosen model on subsamples to check whether the persistence partly reflects shifts in volatility between eras, and compare the models on out-of-sample volatility forecasts rather than in-sample fit alone.

### Analysis

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# packages for the variance models (both used in the notes and the ARCH/GARCH guide)

library(rugarch)
library(FinTS)
```

The series modelled is the monthly change in the yield, in percentage points, from April 1975 onwards. Changes in percentage points are the usual measure for yields, since the price change of a bond is approximately proportional to the change in its yield. Log changes measure relative changes, which assumes that the size of a change scales with the level of the yield. Over this sample the yield ranges from about 7% to 18%, so log changes would shrink the changes of the 1980s and 1990s relative to later years and build a level effect into the volatility, which is something to test rather than assume. Percentage point changes also keep the units consistent with Projects 1 and 4.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# change series and a small ARMA grid for the conditional mean

dy <- diff(za_tbl$yield)

expand_grid(p = 0:2, q = 0:2) |>
  mutate(
    fit = map2(p, q, \(p, q) arima(dy, order = c(p, 0, q))),
    aic = map_dbl(fit, AIC),
    bic = map_dbl(fit, BIC)
  ) |>
  select(-fit) |>
  arrange(bic) |>
  mutate(across(c(aic, bic), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  kable(caption = "Candidate ARMA(p, q) mean models for the yield changes.")
```

The mean model is MA(1), chosen from the ACF of the changes in the exploratory analysis. Both criteria support it: MA(1) has the lowest BIC (511.9) and the lowest AIC (498.7). The next best models by BIC, MA(2) and ARMA(1,1), are about 5.4 higher, and the white noise model is about 56 higher.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# fit the chosen mean model and keep its residuals

mean_order <- c(0, 1)

mean_fit <- arima(dy, order = c(mean_order[1], 0, mean_order[2]))
e_hat <- as.numeric(residuals(mean_fit))

# the first month is lost to differencing
za_res <- tibble(month = za_ts$month[-1], e = e_hat) |>
  as_tsibble(index = month)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# correlograms of the mean residuals and of their squares

za_res |>
  feasts::ACF(e, lag_max = 24) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "ACF of mean model residuals")

za_res |>
  feasts::ACF(e^2, lag_max = 24) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "ACF of squared mean model residuals")
```

The residuals of the MA(1) model show no autocorrelation: every lag up to 24 is inside the bounds except lag 9 (about -0.10), which is borderline. The squared residuals behave differently. Their autocorrelations are about 0.15, 0.15, 0.13 and 0.12 at lags 1 to 4, all outside the bounds, and close to zero after that. Large changes of either sign tend to be followed by large changes for a few months, which is volatility clustering.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# tests for remaining linear structure and for ARCH effects, at 12 lags

lb_e <- Box.test(e_hat, lag = 12, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = sum(mean_order))
lb_e2 <- Box.test(e_hat^2, lag = 12, type = "Ljung-Box")
lm_e <- ArchTest(e_hat, lags = 12)

tibble(
  test = c("Ljung-Box, residuals", "Ljung-Box, squared residuals", "Engle ARCH LM"),
  statistic = c(lb_e$statistic, lb_e2$statistic, lm_e$statistic),
  df = c(lb_e$parameter, lb_e2$parameter, lm_e$parameter),
  p_value = c(lb_e$p.value, lb_e2$p.value, lm_e$p.value)
) |>
  mutate(statistic = round(statistic, 3), p_value = signif(p_value, 3)) |>
  kable(caption = "Tests on the residuals of the mean model.")
```

The Ljung-Box test on the residuals (Q = 12.29, 11 degrees of freedom, p = 0.34) does not reject the null of no autocorrelation, so the MA(1) mean model is adequate. The Ljung-Box test on the squared residuals (Q = 50.1, 12 degrees of freedom, p < 0.001) and Engle's LM test (33.4, 12 degrees of freedom, p < 0.001) both reject the null of no ARCH effects. The conditional variance of the changes is therefore time-varying, which justifies fitting GARCH models.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# normal quantile plot of the mean residuals

tibble(e = e_hat) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = e)) +
  stat_qq(size = 0.8) +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "Normal quantile plot of mean model residuals", x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Sample quantile")
```

The points follow the line in the centre but bend away at both ends in an S shape: the largest fall and rise, about -2.2 and +1.9 percentage points, sit at theoretical quantiles near -3 and +3, far beyond what a normal distribution with the same spread allows. The residuals are therefore heavy-tailed. Part of this can come from the time-varying variance itself, since a mixture of normal distributions with different variances has heavier tails than a single normal. Whether a GARCH model with normal innovations accounts for all of it is checked below by comparing normal and Student t innovations.

Four variance models are fitted, each jointly with the ARMA mean: GARCH(1,1) and GJR-GARCH(1,1), each with normal and Student t innovations.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# specify and fit the four models

make_spec <- \(model, dist) ugarchspec(
  variance.model = list(model = model, garchOrder = c(1, 1)),
  mean.model = list(armaOrder = mean_order, include.mean = TRUE),
  distribution.model = dist
)

models <- tribble(
  ~ name, ~ model, ~ dist,
  "GARCH normal", "sGARCH", "norm",
  "GARCH t", "sGARCH", "std",
  "GJR normal", "gjrGARCH", "norm",
  "GJR t", "gjrGARCH", "std"
)

garch_fits <- map2(models$model, models$dist, \(m, d) ugarchfit(make_spec(m, d), data = dy, solver = "hybrid")) |>
  set_names(models$name)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# coefficient estimates with robust standard errors

# rugarch names: omega is alpha_0, gamma1 is the asymmetry term, shape is the t degrees of freedom
imap_dfr(garch_fits, \(f, nm) {
  m <- f@fit$robust.matcoef
  tibble(model = nm, term = rownames(m), estimate = m[, 1], robust_se = m[, 2], p_value = m[, 4])
}) |>
  mutate(across(c(estimate, robust_se), \(x) round(x, 4)), p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(caption = "Estimates with robust standard errors.")
```

The mean equation is almost the same in all four models: the MA(1) coefficient is about 0.31 (robust standard error about 0.04), close to the 0.34 in Project 1, and the constant mu is not significantly different from zero. In the GARCH t model, alpha1 = 0.19 (robust standard error 0.07) measures how strongly the variance reacts to last month's squared shock, and beta1 = 0.72 (0.11) measures how much of last month's variance carries over. With normal innovations alpha1 is similar (0.21) but beta1 is much lower (0.48), so volatility dies out faster. A likely reason is that the normal model must explain extreme months through spikes in the variance, which then have to decay quickly, while the t distribution can treat some of them as draws from its heavier tails. The asymmetry term gamma1 is close to zero with a large standard error in both GJR models (0.007 with standard error 0.11, and 0.004 with standard error 0.08, both p > 0.95), so there is no evidence of asymmetry. The t degrees of freedom are about 5.3 (robust standard error 1.5), which indicates heavy tails. The fourth moment exists when the degrees of freedom exceed 4, and the implied excess kurtosis of the innovations is 6/(5.3 - 4) ≈ 4.6, although this is imprecise given the standard error.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# model comparison: likelihood, information criteria and persistence

# rugarch reports information criteria per observation
imap_dfr(garch_fits, \(f, nm) tibble(
  model = nm,
  loglik = likelihood(f),
  aic = infocriteria(f)[1],
  bic = infocriteria(f)[2],
  persistence = as.numeric(persistence(f)),
  half_life = as.numeric(halflife(f)),
  long_run_sd = sqrt(as.numeric(uncvariance(f)))
)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Model comparison.")
```

All three criteria prefer the Student t models. Replacing the normal with the t distribution raises the log-likelihood by about 26 for one extra parameter, and lowers AIC from 0.712 to 0.629 and BIC from 0.748 to 0.672 (rugarch reports both per observation). Adding the asymmetry term changes the log-likelihood by less than 0.01 and raises both criteria, so GARCH t is preferred overall. Persistence (alpha1 + beta1) is 0.91 in the t models, so the gap between the conditional and the long-run variance halves in about 7.5 months. In the normal models it is 0.69, a half-life of about 1.9 months. The long-run standard deviation of the GARCH t model, 0.40 percentage points, is close to the sample standard deviation of the changes (0.38). A persistence of 0.91 is not close enough to one to suggest an integrated GARCH, but shifts in the average level of volatility between eras can still inflate estimated persistence, so refitting on subsamples would be a useful check.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# diagnostics on the standardised residuals of each model (p-values, 12 lags)

imap_dfr(garch_fits, \(f, nm) {
  z <- as.numeric(residuals(f, standardize = TRUE))
  tibble(
    model = nm,
    lb_z = Box.test(z, lag = 12, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = sum(mean_order))$p.value,
    lb_z_sq = Box.test(z^2, lag = 12, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value,
    arch_lm = as.numeric(ArchTest(z, lags = 12)$p.value)
  )
}) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "Diagnostic p-values: Ljung-Box on z, Ljung-Box on z squared, ARCH LM on z.")
```

The four models give almost identical diagnostics. The Ljung-Box test on the standardised residuals (p ≈ 0.44) shows no remaining autocorrelation in the mean, and the Ljung-Box test on their squares and the ARCH LM test (p ≈ 0.998) show no remaining ARCH effects. Every model removes the volatility clustering found in the mean model residuals, so the diagnostics do not distinguish between them, and the choice rests on the likelihood and the fit in the tails.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# quantile plots of standardised residuals against each model's own innovation distribution

imap_dfr(garch_fits, \(f, nm) {
  z <- sort(as.numeric(residuals(f, standardize = TRUE)))
  p <- ppoints(length(z))
  # qdist gives the unit variance t that rugarch garch_fits
  theo <- if ("shape" %in% names(coef(f))) qdist("std", p, shape = coef(f)["shape"]) else qnorm(p)
  tibble(model = nm, theoretical = theo, sample = z)
}) |>
  ggplot(aes(theoretical, sample)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(title = "Quantile plots of standardised residuals", x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Sample quantile")
```

The Student t fits the tails better. Under the normal models the largest standardised residuals lie well above the line, at about 4.2 and 6.8 against theoretical values below 3.2, while under the t models the points stay close to the line except for the single largest value. That one month is extreme under every model, at about 7 to 8 standard deviations, so even the t distribution does not fully capture the largest shock, most likely the rise in early 2020 that followed a calm period.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# news impact curves for the symmetric and asymmetric models

map_dfr(c("GARCH t", "GJR t"), \(nm) {
  ni <- newsimpact(z = NULL, garch_fits[[nm]])
  tibble(model = nm, shock = ni$zx, variance = ni$zy)
}) |>
  ggplot(aes(shock, variance, linetype = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "News impact curves", x = "Shock at t - 1", y = "Conditional variance at t")
```

There is no evidence of asymmetry: the two news impact curves lie on top of each other and are symmetric about zero, consistent with gamma1 being close to zero. In the rugarch GJR model the extra term applies to negative shocks, which for a yield are unexpected falls, that is, rises in bond prices. A common hypothesis is that unexpected rises in yields, which mean losses for bondholders, raise volatility more, which would give a negative gamma1. The estimates support neither direction.

The remaining chunks use the GARCH(1,1) model with Student t innovations. It has the lowest AIC and BIC of the four models. GJR t has a log-likelihood higher by only about 0.001, because its asymmetry term is negligible and only adds a parameter. The diagnostics are equally good for all four models, and the t innovations fit the tails better than the normal.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# changes against the fitted conditional mean plus and minus two conditional standard deviations

chosen <- "GARCH t"

tibble(
  date = za_tbl$date[-1],
  change = dy,
  mu = as.numeric(fitted(garch_fits[[chosen]])),
  s = as.numeric(sigma(garch_fits[[chosen]]))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = change), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mu + 2 * s), colour = "blue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mu - 2 * s), colour = "blue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(title = paste("Yield changes with two conditional SD band:", chosen), x = NULL, y = "percentage points")
```

The two standard deviation band is narrowest, at about ±0.5 percentage points, in the late 1970s and for much of the 2000s and 2010s. It widens sharply after large shocks: in the early and mid-1980s, around 1998, when the lower band reaches about -2.9, and in 2020, when the upper band reaches about 2.3. After each spike the band narrows over several months rather than at once, which is the persistence measured by beta1. The band follows the clusters of large changes in the data, which a constant variance model cannot do.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# 24 month conditional standard deviation forecast, with the long run level marked

garch_fc <- ugarchforecast(garch_fits[[chosen]], n.ahead = 24)

tibble(h = 1:24, sd = as.numeric(sigma(garch_fc))) |>
  ggplot(aes(h, sd)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sqrt(as.numeric(uncvariance(garch_fits[[chosen]]))), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = paste("Forecast conditional SD:", chosen), x = "Months ahead", y = "percentage points")
```

The forecast starts at about 0.408 percentage points one month ahead, only slightly above the long-run level of 0.397, so volatility at the end of the sample (June 2026) is close to its long-run average. It declines smoothly towards the long-run level, closing half the remaining gap in the variance about every 7.5 months, and at 24 months (0.398) it has almost reached it. Because the starting level is so close to the long-run level, the forecast adds little to the unconditional standard deviation at any horizon. After a volatile period the forecast would start higher and the rate of reversion would matter more.

### Discussion

Monthly changes in the South African 10-year yield have a time-varying conditional variance. GARCH(1,1) with Student t innovations describes it well: it removes the ARCH effects, fits the tails better than normal innovations, and shows volatility that rises after large shocks and then decays, with a half-life of about 7.5 months. There is no evidence of asymmetry.

Several limitations apply. Monthly data, and especially monthly averages, smooth out movements within the month, so the model describes volatility at a monthly scale only. The sample spans several monetary regimes, and a GARCH model with fixed parameters treats shifts in the average level of volatility as persistent shocks, which may overstate persistence. The model was also chosen on in-sample fit rather than forecasting performance.

[Project 4](#sec-project-4) takes a different view. Instead of volatility that evolves smoothly with each shock, it allows the changes to switch between a small number of regimes with different volatilities. Comparing the periods the hidden Markov model assigns to its high-volatility state with the spikes in the GARCH band shows whether the two views agree.

## Project 3: Harmonic regression for a seasonal temperature series {#sec-project-3}

### Summary

- Section and topic: Section 2, harmonic (Fourier) regression with ARMA errors, supported by the periodogram
- Type: implementation on real-world data
- Question: how many harmonic terms does the annual temperature cycle need, and does a harmonic regression with ARMA errors forecast as well as a SARIMA model?
- Data: average monthly air temperature at Nottingham Castle, 1920 to 1939, in degrees Fahrenheit (R dataset `nottem`, 240 months), with the last 24 months held out
- Methods: periodogram, harmonic regression with K = 0 to 6 Fourier pairs and ARMA errors chosen by AICc, SARIMA baseline, test-set accuracy and prediction interval coverage
- Key findings: **key findings**
- What I would do differently: **what you would do differently next time**

### Analysis

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# forecast is used for Arima/auto.arima with xreg, fourier() and accuracy()
# it is loaded after fabletools, so its functions are called with forecast:: to avoid masking confusion

library(forecast)
```

The bond yield shows virtually no seasonal component, so harmonic terms have nothing to describe there. **Evidence for this, for example the seasonal naive results in Project 1 or a periodogram of the yield changes** This project therefore uses a series with a strong, regular annual cycle, the Nottingham Castle temperature series. Its training and test sets and exploratory analysis are in the [Data](#sec-temp-data) section.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# raw periodogram of the linearly detrended training series
# frequency is in cycles per year because the ts has frequency 12

pg <- spec.pgram(y_train, detrend = TRUE, taper = 0.1, plot = FALSE)

pg_tbl <- tibble(freq = pg$freq, spec = pg$spec) |>
  mutate(period_months = 12 / freq, share = spec / sum(spec))

# dotted lines mark the seasonal frequencies 1, 2, ..., 6 cycles per year

ggplot(pg_tbl, aes(freq, spec)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1:6, linetype = "dotted", colour = "blue") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Periodogram of the training series", x = "frequency (cycles per year)", y = "spectrum (log scale)")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# largest periodogram ordinates

pg_tbl |>
  slice_max(spec, n = 6) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Six largest periodogram ordinates.")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# periodogram ordinates at the seasonal frequencies, which are the ones fourier() can represent

idx_seasonal <- sapply(1:6, \(j) which.min(abs(pg$freq - j)))

pg_tbl |>
  slice(idx_seasonal) |>
  mutate(harmonic = 1:6, .before = 1) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "Periodogram ordinates at the seasonal frequencies.")
```

The two tables show where the power sits and how much of it falls at the seasonal frequencies j/12 that the Fourier terms use. **Interpretation of the periodogram: the dominant period in months, whether the smaller peaks are harmonics of the annual cycle (2, 3, ... cycles per year) or separate cycles, and how much of the variance sits at the seasonal frequencies**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# fit a harmonic regression with K Fourier pairs and stationary ARMA errors
# d = 0 keeps the errors ARMA, so AICc is comparable across K
# K = 0 is the same model with no harmonics, included as a reference

fit_k <- function(K) {
  xr <- if (K == 0) NULL else forecast::fourier(y_train, K = K)
  forecast::auto.arima(y_train, xreg = xr, d = 0, seasonal = FALSE, stepwise = FALSE, approximation = FALSE)
}

# full search over ARMA orders for each K, this can take a minute or two

hr_fits <- map(0:6, fit_k)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# AICc and the selected ARMA error orders for each K

aicc_tbl <- tibble(
  K = 0:6,
  error_model = map_chr(hr_fits, \(f) paste0("ARMA(", f$arma[1], ",", f$arma[2], ")")),
  n_coef = map_int(hr_fits, \(f) length(coef(f))),
  sigma2 = map_dbl(hr_fits, \(f) f$sigma2),
  aicc = map_dbl(hr_fits, \(f) f$aicc)
)

aicc_tbl |>
  mutate(across(c(sigma2, aicc), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "AICc by number of harmonics K.")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# keep the best model with at least one harmonic

K_best <- aicc_tbl |>
  filter(K >= 1) |>
  slice_min(aicc, n = 1) |>
  pull(K)

fit_hr <- hr_fits[[K_best + 1]]

tibble(term = names(coef(fit_hr)),
  estimate = coef(fit_hr),
  se = sqrt(diag(fit_hr$var.coef))
) |>
  mutate(z = estimate / se) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = paste0("Harmonic regression with ARMA errors, K = ", K_best, "."))
```

Also justify d = 0 from the trend check in the [Data](#sec-temp-data) section rather than assuming it**

## Project 4: Hidden Markov model for regimes in yield changes {#sec-project-4}

### Summary

- Section and topic: Section 2, hidden Markov models
- Type: implementation from first principles on real-world data
- Question: can monthly yield changes be described by a small number of regimes with different means and volatilities, and does a regime model forecast better than an iid normal model?
- Data: monthly changes in the yield from April 1975, with the last 24 months held out
- Methods: Gaussian HMM likelihood by the scaled forward algorithm, numerical maximisation from several starting values, number of states chosen by AIC and BIC, Viterbi and forward-backward decoding, mixture forecast distributions, one-step-ahead evaluation by coverage and log score, simulated level forecasts, check against depmixS4
- Key findings: **key findings**
- What I would do differently: **what you would do differently next time**

### Analysis

#### Yield changes

#### Training and test split

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

n_test <- 24
y_all <- as.numeric(dy_ts)
n <- length(y_all)
nx_train <- n - n_test
x_train <- y_all[1:nx_train]
x_test <- y_all[(nx_train + 1):n]
t_all <- as.numeric(time(dy_ts))
```

#### Parameter transformations

Means are unconstrained, standard deviations are estimated on the log scale, and the off-diagonal entries of $\Gamma$ use a multinomial logit with the diagonal as reference. $\delta$ is the stationary distribution of $\Gamma$.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

n2w <- function(mu, sigma, gamma) {
  m <- length(mu)
  tgamma <- NULL
  if (m > 1) {
    # divides row i by gamma_ii
    tgamma <- log(gamma / diag(gamma))
    tgamma <- tgamma[!diag(m)]
  }
  c(mu, log(sigma), tgamma)
}

w2n <- function(par, m) {
  mu <- par[1:m]
  sigma <- exp(par[(m + 1):(2 * m)])
  gamma <- diag(m)
  if (m > 1) {
    gamma[!gamma] <- exp(par[(2 * m + 1):(m * (m + 1))])
    gamma <- gamma / rowSums(gamma)
  }
  delta <- if (m > 1) solve(t(diag(m) - gamma + 1), rep(1, m)) else 1
  list(mu = mu, sigma = sigma, gamma = gamma, delta = delta)
}
```

#### Negative log-likelihood (scaled forward algorithm)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

hmm_nll <- function(par, x, m) {
  p <- w2n(par, m)
  phi <- p$delta
  ll <- 0
  for (t in seq_along(x)) {
    v <- phi %*% p$gamma * dnorm(x[t], p$mu, p$sigma)
    u <- sum(v)
    ll <- ll + log(u)
    phi <- v / u
  }
  -ll
}
```

#### Fitting with several starting values

States are relabelled in order of increasing standard deviation, so state 1 is always the calmest.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

fit_hmm <- function(x, m, n_starts = 20) {
  best <- NULL
  for (s in 1:n_starts) {
    mu0 <- rnorm(m, mean(x), sd(x) / 10)
    sigma0 <- sd(x) * exp(runif(m, -1.5, 1))
    g0 <- matrix(1)
    if (m > 1) {
      d <- runif(m, 0.7, 0.98)
      g0 <- (1 - d) / (m - 1) * matrix(1, m, m)
      diag(g0) <- d
    }
    out <- tryCatch(nlm(hmm_nll, n2w(mu0, sigma0, g0), x = x, m = m,
                        iterlim = 1000),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(out) && (is.null(best) || out$minimum < best$minimum)) {
      best <- out
    }
  }
  p <- w2n(best$estimate, m)
  ord <- order(p$sigma)
  list(mu = p$mu[ord], sigma = p$sigma[ord], gamma = p$gamma[ord, ord, drop = FALSE],
       delta = p$delta[ord], nll = best$minimum, k = m * (m + 1), code = best$code)
}
```

#### Number of states

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

set.seed(2026)
hmm_fits <- lapply(1:3, function(m) fit_hmm(x_train, m))

sel <- data.frame(m = 1:3,
                  k = sapply(hmm_fits, `[[`, "k"),
                  logLik = -sapply(hmm_fits, `[[`, "nll"),
                  code = sapply(hmm_fits, `[[`, "code"))
sel$AIC <- -2 * sel$logLik + 2 * sel$k
sel$BIC <- -2 * sel$logLik + log(nx_train) * sel$k

sel |>
  mutate(across(c(logLik, AIC, BIC), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  kable(caption = "Number of states: log-likelihood, AIC and BIC. code is the nlm convergence code (1 or 2 indicates probable convergence).")
```

**Interpretation: the number of states chosen by BIC, and whether AIC agrees**

```{r}

#| message: false

hmm_fit <- hmm_fits[[m_hat]]

tibble(state = 1:m_hat, mean = hmm_fit$mu, sd = hmm_fit$sigma, stationary_prob = hmm_fit$delta) |>
  mutate(across(-state, \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(caption = "State-dependent means and standard deviations (percentage points), and the stationary distribution.")

gamma_tbl <- round(hmm_fit$gamma, 4)
dimnames(gamma_tbl) <- list(paste("from state", 1:m_hat), paste("to state", 1:m_hat))
kable(gamma_tbl, caption = "Estimated transition probability matrix.")
```

**Interpretation of the state means, standard deviations, transition probabilities (expected duration 1 / (1 - gamma_ii) months) and stationary distribution**

#### Global decoding (Viterbi)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

viterbi_norm <- function(x, fit) {
  m <- length(fit$mu)
  n <- length(x)
  lg <- log(fit$gamma)
  lp <- outer(x, 1:m, function(x, i) dnorm(x, fit$mu[i], fit$sigma[i], log = TRUE))
  xi <- matrix(0, n, m)
  xi[1, ] <- log(fit$delta) + lp[1, ]
  for (t in 2:n) {
    for (j in 1:m) {
      xi[t, j] <- max(xi[t - 1, ] + lg[, j]) + lp[t, j]
    }
  }
  s <- numeric(n)
  s[n] <- which.max(xi[n, ])
  for (t in (n - 1):1) {
    s[t] <- which.max(xi[t, ] + lg[, s[t + 1]])
  }
  s
}

vit <- viterbi_norm(x_train, hmm_fit)
```

#### Local decoding (scaled forward-backward)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

log_fb <- function(x, fit) {
  m <- length(fit$mu)
  n <- length(x)
  P <- outer(x, 1:m, function(x, i) dnorm(x, fit$mu[i], fit$sigma[i]))
  la <- lb <- matrix(0, n, m)

  phi <- fit$delta * P[1, ]
  lscale <- log(sum(phi))
  phi <- phi / sum(phi)
  la[1, ] <- lscale + log(phi)
  for (t in 2:n) {
    phi <- phi %*% fit$gamma * P[t, ]
    lscale <- lscale + log(sum(phi))
    phi <- phi / sum(phi)
    la[t, ] <- lscale + log(phi)
  }

  # beta_T = 1, stored as phi = 1/m with log scale log(m)
  phi <- rep(1 / m, m)
  lscale <- log(m)
  for (t in (n - 1):1) {
    phi <- fit$gamma %*% (P[t + 1, ] * phi)
    lb[t, ] <- log(phi) + lscale
    lscale <- lscale + log(sum(phi))
    phi <- phi / sum(phi)
  }
  list(la = la, lb = lb)
}

state_probs <- function(x, fit) {
  fb <- log_fb(x, fit)
  la_n <- fb$la[length(x), ]
  llk <- max(la_n) + log(sum(exp(la_n - max(la_n))))
  exp(fb$la + fb$lb - llk)
}

smooth_probs <- state_probs(x_train, hmm_fit)
```

**Interpretation: which historical periods fall in each state, linked to the era boundaries in the exploratory analysis**

#### Forecast distribution

The h-step forecast distribution is a normal mixture with weights $\phi_T \Gamma^h$, where $\phi_T$ are the filtered state probabilities at the end of the training period.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

filter_probs <- function(x, fit) {
  la <- log_fb(x, fit)$la
  # subtract each row's maximum before exponentiating
  f <- exp(la - apply(la, 1, max))
  f / rowSums(f)
}

mix_quantile <- function(p, w, mu, sigma) {
  f <- function(q) sum(w * pnorm(q, mu, sigma)) - p
  uniroot(f, range(mu) + c(-10, 10) * max(sigma))$root
}

fc_hmm <- function(fit, phi, h_max, level = 0.95) {
  a <- (1 - level) / 2
  w <- phi
  out <- matrix(NA, h_max, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mean", "lower", "upper")))
  for (h in 1:h_max) {
    w <- w %*% fit$gamma
    out[h, ] <- c(sum(w * fit$mu),
                  mix_quantile(a, w, fit$mu, fit$sigma),
                  mix_quantile(1 - a, w, fit$mu, fit$sigma))
  }
  out
}

filt_all <- filter_probs(y_all, hmm_fit)
hmm_fc <- fc_hmm(hmm_fit, filt_all[nx_train, ], n_test)
iid_fc <- fc_hmm(hmm_fits[[1]], 1, n_test)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

t_test <- t_all[(nx_train + 1):n]
t_recent <- t_all > 2018

plot(t_all[t_recent], y_all[t_recent], type = "l", las = 1,
     ylim = range(y_all[t_recent], hmm_fc, iid_fc),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Change in yield (percentage points)")

lines(t_test, hmm_fc[, "upper"], col = "red", lty = 2)
lines(t_test, iid_fc[, "lower"], col = "steelblue", lty = 3)
lines(t_test, iid_fc[, "upper"], col = "steelblue", lty = 3)
abline(v = t_test[1], col = "grey")
legend("topleft", legend = c(paste0(m_hat, "-state HMM"), "1-state (iid normal)"),
       col = c("red", "steelblue"), lty = c(2, 3), bty = "n")
```

#### One-step-ahead evaluation on the test set

Parameters are held at their training estimates. The filter is updated with each new observation, and each one-step forecast is compared with the next observed change. Coverage is of the 95% interval; the log score is the mean log predictive density.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

one_step_eval <- function(fit, filt) {
  res <- t(sapply(nx_train:(n - 1), function(t) {
    w <- filt[t, ] %*% fit$gamma
    c(fc_hmm(fit, filt[t, ], 1),
      log(sum(w * dnorm(y_all[t + 1], fit$mu, fit$sigma))))
  }))
  c(coverage = mean(x_test >= res[, 2] & x_test <= res[, 3]),
    mean_width = mean(res[, 3] - res[, 2]),
    log_score = mean(res[, 4]))
}

rbind(hmm = one_step_eval(hmm_fit, filt_all),
      iid_normal = one_step_eval(hmm_fits[[1]], filter_probs(y_all, hmm_fits[[1]]))) |>
  round(4) |>
  kable(caption = "One-step-ahead evaluation on the test months: coverage of the 95% interval, mean interval width and mean log score.")
```

**Interpretation of coverage, interval width and log score for the HMM against the iid normal model**

#### Yield level forecasts by simulation

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

sim_paths <- function(fit, phi, h_max, n_sim, y0) {
  m <- length(fit$mu)
  paths <- matrix(NA, n_sim, h_max)
  for (s in 1:n_sim) {
    state <- sample(1:m, 1, prob = phi)
    level <- y0
    for (h in 1:h_max) {
      state <- sample(1:m, 1, prob = fit$gamma[state, ])
      level <- level + rnorm(1, fit$mu[state], fit$sigma[state])
      paths[s, h] <- level
    }
  }
  paths
}

set.seed(2026)
y_levels <- as.numeric(y_ts)
y0 <- y_levels[nx_train + 1]
band <- apply(sim_paths(hmm_fit, filt_all[nx_train, ], n_test, 5000, y0), 2,
              quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
band1 <- apply(sim_paths(hmm_fits[[1]], 1, n_test, 5000, y0), 2,
               quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
```

#### Check against depmixS4

depmixS4 estimates the initial distribution freely rather than setting it to the stationary distribution, so the log-likelihoods should be close but not identical. State labels may differ, so compare the Viterbi paths with a cross-table.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(depmixS4)

set.seed(1)
mod <- depmix(dy_ts ~ 1, data = data.frame(dy_ts = x_train), nstates = m_hat,
              family = gaussian())
fm <- fit(mod, verbose = FALSE)

tibble(fit = c("own", "depmixS4"), logLik = c(-hmm_fit$nll, as.numeric(logLik(fm)))) |>
  kable(caption = "Log-likelihood of the two fits.")
summary(fm)
table(own = vit, depmixS4 = fm@posterior$state)
```

# Tutorials {#sec-tutorials}

## Section overviews

### Section 1

**Overview of Section 1: key concepts, the most challenging aspects, and your understanding**

### Section 2

**Overview of Section 2: key concepts, the most challenging aspects, and your understanding**

## Tutorial 1: The forecasting process and features of time series {#sec-tut-1}

**Brief statement of each question, so the answers can be read on their own**

### Question 1

Problem definition. Establish what the forecasts are for and who will use them. For a biscuit manufacturer this is likely production scheduling, purchasing of raw materials (flour, sugar, chocolate, packaging), inventory and distribution planning, and budgeting. This determines which products are forecast, the level of aggregation (individual SKU, product family, region or retailer), the forecast horizon (weeks for production runs, months for procurement, a year or more for capacity and budgets), how often forecasts are updated, and how accurate they need to be. It requires discussion with production, sales, marketing and finance staff.

Data collection. Gather historical sales for each product at the frequency and aggregation chosen above, ideally covering several years so that seasonal patterns can be estimated. Decide whether to use orders, shipments or retail sales, since shipments can understate true demand during stock-outs. Collect related information that may explain sales: prices, promotions, advertising, public holidays and festive periods, product launches and discontinuations, and competitor activity. Expert knowledge from the sales team about planned promotions or contracts is also data. Check for errors, gaps and changes in definitions.

Data analysis. Plot each series and look for trend, seasonality (for example peaks before Christmas and Easter), cycles, outliers, and structural breaks such as a product relaunch or a lost retail contract. Examine autocorrelation and relationships between sales and explanatory variables such as price or promotions, and between products (cannibalisation). Decide whether a transformation is needed, for example logs if variability grows with the level of sales. The feedback arrow in Figure 1 reflects that this step is revisited when fitted models reveal something missed.

Model selection and fitting. Using what the analysis showed, choose candidate models: simple benchmarks (naive, seasonal naive), moving averages, exponential smoothing (for example Holt-Winters for trend and seasonality), ARIMA or SARIMA models, or regression models with promotion and price effects. Because there are several products, methods that can be applied systematically across many series are attractive. Estimate the parameters of each candidate on the training data.

Model validation. Assess how well each model forecasts data it was not fitted to, using a hold-out test set or rolling-origin evaluation. Compare accuracy measures such as MAE, RMSE, MAPE or MASE, including against the benchmark methods. Check the residuals: they should look like uncorrelated noise with mean zero (for example using the residual ACF and a Ljung-Box test). Also check whether prediction intervals have roughly the stated coverage. Select the model or models to use.

Forecasting model deployment. Put the chosen model into routine use: refit it on all available data, produce point forecasts and prediction intervals at the required horizon and frequency, and deliver them in a form the planners can use, ideally integrated with the company’s planning systems. Document the method and assumptions, and allow for judgemental adjustment where planners know of future events the model cannot see, such as a planned promotion.

Monitoring forecasting model performance. As actual sales arrive, compare them to the forecasts and track the errors over time to detect bias or declining accuracy. Changes in consumer tastes, pricing, competitors or distribution can make a model inadequate. When performance deteriorates, re-estimate or re-specify the model, which returns the process to earlier stages.

### Question 2

a)  Monthly computer hard drive sales, 10 years, local store. A trend is likely: growth as computer use increased, possibly followed by decline as solid-state drives and cloud storage replaced hard drives. Annual seasonality is likely, with peaks around the start of the academic year and the end-of-year festive and Black Friday period. Some cyclical behaviour linked to economic conditions is also possible.

b)  Hourly pulse rate, one week. No long-term trend. A strong daily (24-hour) pattern is expected: lower during sleep and higher during waking hours. There will be short-lived spikes from exercise or stress and strong autocorrelation between adjacent hours. A weekday versus weekend difference may exist, but one week of data is too short to estimate a weekly pattern.

c)  Daily fast-food sales, six months. A strong weekly seasonal pattern is expected, with higher sales on particular days such as Fridays and weekends. There may be a trend over the period, and effects from public holidays, school holidays, paydays and promotions. Annual seasonality cannot be identified from six months; part of it may appear as a trend.

d)  Weekly electricity consumption, local area, 10 years. Strong annual seasonality driven by heating in winter and cooling in summer (with a period of about 52.18 weeks, which is not an integer). A trend is possible, upward from population and economic growth or downward from efficiency improvements and rooftop solar. Dips over the Christmas and New Year period, and irregular variation from unusual weather, are also expected.

### Question 6

Time plot. The series does not fluctuate around a constant mean. It rises from about 460 to about 600 over the first 110 or so days, drifts down, then falls sharply to about 310 around days 240 to 270 before levelling off near 350 to 400. These long runs and level shifts, with no tendency to return to a fixed level, are typical of a random walk rather than a stationary process.

ACF. The autocorrelations are close to 1 at lag 1 and decay very slowly, roughly linearly, remaining around 0.8 at lag 25 and far outside the significance bounds. For a stationary series the ACF should decay to zero fairly quickly. Slow decay of this kind indicates non-stationarity.

PACF. There is a single large spike at lag 1 with a value close to 1, and the remaining partial autocorrelations are essentially within the bounds. This is consistent with an AR(1) process with coefficient close to 1, that is, a unit root.

Conclusion. Together the plots indicate that the series is non-stationary in the mean and that first differencing, $y'_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$, is appropriate. The differenced series (daily price changes) would be expected to look approximately like white noise. A unit root test such as ADF or KPSS could be used to support this formally.

### Reflection

**Reflection: what you learned, what was difficult, and how it fed into the projects**

## Tutorial 2: Exponential smoothing {#sec-tut-2}

**Brief statement of each question**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(fpp2)
```

### Question 1

Own implementation of SES. `ses_onestep()` runs the recursion $\hat{y}_{t+1|t} = \alpha y_t + (1 - \alpha)\hat{y}_{t|t-1}$ with $\hat{y}_{1|0} = \ell_0$ and returns all one-step-ahead forecasts, the last of which is the forecast of the next observation.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ses_onestep <- function(y, alpha, level) {
  n <- length(y)
  yhat <- numeric(n + 1)
  yhat[1] <- level
  for (t in 1:n) yhat[t + 1] <- alpha * y[t] + (1 - alpha) * yhat[t]
  yhat
}

ses_fc <- function(y, alpha, level) {
  tail(ses_onestep(y, alpha, level), 1)
}

ses_sse <- function(par, y) {
  yhat <- ses_onestep(y, par[1], par[2])
  sum((y - yhat[seq_along(y)])^2)
}
```

Estimate $\alpha$ and $\ell_0$ by minimising the SSE, and fit `ses()` for comparison.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
est_m <- optim(c(0.5, marathon[1]), ses_sse, y = marathon)
fit_m <- ses(marathon, h = 1)

rbind(optim = est_m$par, ses = fit_m$model$par[c("alpha", "l")])
```

Forecast for 2017 from the own function (with the `optim` estimates and with the `ses()` estimates) against `ses()`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
alpha_m <- unname(fit_m$model$par["alpha"])
l0_m <- unname(fit_m$model$par["l"])

c(own_optim = ses_fc(marathon, est_m$par[1], est_m$par[2]),
  own_ses_par = ses_fc(marathon, alpha_m, l0_m),
  ses = fit_m$mean[1])
```

Point forecast and 95% prediction interval for 2017 by hand, using $\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{SSE / (T - 2)}$ (two estimated parameters).

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
n_m <- length(marathon)
res_m <- marathon - ses_onestep(marathon, alpha_m, l0_m)[1:n_m]
sigma_m <- sqrt(sum(res_m^2) / (n_m - 2))
fc_m <- ses_fc(marathon, alpha_m, l0_m)

pi_m <- rbind(own = c(fc_m, fc_m + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sigma_m),
              ses = c(fit_m$mean[1], fit_m$lower[1, "95%"], fit_m$upper[1, "95%"]))
colnames(pi_m) <- c("forecast", "lower", "upper")
pi_m
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
plot(marathon, las = 1, ylab = "Winning time (minutes)", xlab = "Year")
lines(fitted(fit_m), col = "red")
```

```{r}

#| warning: false

```

### Question 5

Simulate from the innovations state-space form of SES: $y_t = \ell_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, $\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha \varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$, with $\alpha = 0.3$, $\ell_0 = 50$, $\sigma = 2$.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
sim_ses <- function(n, alpha, l0, sigma) {
  y <- numeric(n)
  level <- l0
  for (t in 1:n) {
    e <- rnorm(1, 0, sigma)
    y[t] <- level + e
    level <- level + alpha * e
  }
  ts(y)
}

set.seed(2026)
y_ses <- sim_ses(n = 200, alpha = 0.3, l0 = 50, sigma = 2)
plot(y_ses, las = 1, ylab = "y")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
est_s <- optim(c(0.5, y_ses[1]), ses_sse, y = y_ses)
fit_s <- ses(y_ses)

rbind(true = c(alpha = 0.3, l = 50, sigma = 2),
      optim = c(est_s$par, sqrt(est_s$value / (length(y_ses) - 2))),
      ses = c(fit_s$model$par[c("alpha", "l")], sqrt(fit_s$model$sigma2)))
```

**Comment on how well the true SES parameters are recovered**

Holt's method in the same form: $y_t = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, $\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + \alpha \varepsilon_t$, $b_t = b_{t-1} + \beta \varepsilon_t$, with $\alpha = 0.3$, $\beta = 0.05$, $\ell_0 = 50$, $b_0 = 0.5$, $\sigma = 2$. `holt()` reports $\beta$ in this parametrisation.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
sim_holt <- function(n, alpha, beta, l0, b0, sigma) {
  y <- numeric(n)
  level <- l0
  trend <- b0
  for (t in 1:n) {
    e <- rnorm(1, 0, sigma)
    y[t] <- level + trend + e
    level <- level + trend + alpha * e
    trend <- trend + beta * e
  }
  ts(y)
}

set.seed(2026)
y_holt <- sim_holt(n = 200, alpha = 0.3, beta = 0.05, l0 = 50, b0 = 0.5, sigma = 2)
plot(y_holt, las = 1, ylab = "y")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
holt_sse <- function(par, y) {
  alpha <- par[1]
  beta <- par[2]
  level <- par[3]
  trend <- par[4]
  sse <- 0
  for (t in seq_along(y)) {
    e <- y[t] - (level + trend)
    sse <- sse + e^2
    level <- level + trend + alpha * e
    trend <- trend + beta * e
  }
  sse
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
est_h <- optim(c(0.5, 0.1, y_holt[1], 0), holt_sse, y = y_holt)
fit_h <- holt(y_holt)

rbind(true = c(alpha = 0.3, beta = 0.05, l = 50, b = 0.5, sigma = 2),
      optim = c(est_h$par, sqrt(est_h$value / (length(y_holt) - 4))),
      holt = c(fit_h$model$par[c("alpha", "beta", "l", "b")], sqrt(fit_h$model$sigma2)))
```

**Comment on how well the true Holt parameters are recovered**

### Basic structural model: co2

The model from the prac is refitted here so that this section runs on its own.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
build_bsm <- function(p) {
  mod <- dlmModPoly() + dlmModSeas(12)
  W(mod)[1, 1] <- exp(p[1])
  W(mod)[2, 2] <- exp(p[2])
  W(mod)[3, 3] <- exp(p[3])
  V(mod) <- exp(p[4])
  mod
}

mle_bsm <- dlmMLE(co2, parm = c(0, 0, 0, 0), build = build_bsm)
mod_bsm <- build_bsm(mle_bsm$par)
filt_bsm <- dlmFilter(co2, mod_bsm)
exp(mle_bsm$par)
```

The filtered states are erratic at the start of the series because the prior is diffuse, with $m_0 = 0$ and $C_0 = 10^7 I_{13}$. The table shows the filtered level, slope and first seasonal state, with the standard error of the level, for the first two years. **Comment on how quickly the filter settles**

```{r}
round(cbind(y = c(NA, co2[1:24]),
            level = filt_bsm$m[1:25, 1], se_level = se_bsm[1:25, 1],
            slope = filt_bsm$m[1:25, 2], season = filt_bsm$m[1:25, 3]), 2)
```
